doc.title: Herb Ellis interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Sight-reading the guitar feature with Jimmy Dorsey
summary: Ellis memorized Dorsey's guitar feature, bluffed his way through on his first night, and later claimed unreadable parts did not lay well.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: Tell us a little about that story you told us you were going to tell us about the Dorsey band.

Oh, yeah. Well I went with Jimmy Dorsey and I played, I had two guitars. I had a rhythm guitar and an electric guitar. So there was a guitar feature in the band and I knew about it. So I got the record before I joined him and I learned it. And it was sort of difficult. It was a chord solo with a few single notes and it was the melody, so you had to play it pretty close to the way it was written you know. And I was a very bad reader in those days. And so we were on the job the first night and Jimmy gave me a couple of solos here and there. And then he pulled this number, “Sorghum Switch” I’ll never forget it was number 43. And so he was about to beat it off and he says, “Oh, Herb, I’m sorry.” He said, “This is a guitar solo and I understand it’s rather difficult,” he says. “Why don’t you just take it home and we’ll play it in a couple of nights now.” I’m looking at it like I could read it see, because I had it memorized. And I said, “No, Jimmy,” I says, “I think I can get through it, let’s try it.” So we did, and I played it perfectly — or almost perfectly. That was the night that the arrangers came in and brought the arrangements and then he’d tell them what they were going to do next. So he got all the arrangements together after that and he said, “I want you to write for Herb.” He said, “I want him playing lead and harmony parts. He can read anything.”
So then did you have to back it up from that point on?

Well yeah, but see I had him so buffaloed by that, that bringing the part that I couldn’t sight read, which was often, I’d tell him that it didn’t lay well, which is a bunch of nonsense. But he believed me. Because he thought if I couldn’t play it right off then it was unplayable, you know. So it worked.
